title: Continual learning and catastrophic forgetting (Bridge to AI)
text:
CHAPTER 11. PLASTICITY AND DEVELOPMENT
SECTION 11.3. CONTINUAL LEARNING AND CATASTROPHIC FORGETTING

The dedicated Bridge to AI for plasticity

You learned to walk as a toddler, to read as a child, and to solve differential equations as a student. Learning each new skill did not erase the previous ones. This seems so natural that we rarely think about it. But for artificial neural networks, it is a serious problem. A network trained on task A and then trained on task B usually forgets task A, often quickly and almost completely. This phenomenon is called catastrophic forgetting or catastrophic interference. Overcoming it, so that a system can learn a sequence of tasks or a continual stream of data over its lifetime, is the goal of continual learning (also called lifelong learning or incremental learning). This section explains why forgetting happens, surveys the main families of solutions, and relates each to mechanisms in the brain that we have met in earlier chapters.

Why networks forget

Recall from section 9.2 that McCloskey and Cohen (1989) and Ratcliff (1990) described catastrophic interference in networks trained with backpropagation. The cause is easy to understand geometrically.

A network's knowledge is stored in its weight vector w, a point in a very high-dimensional space. Training on task A moves w to a region where the loss L_A(w) is low. Training on task B then follows the gradient of L_B(w), moving w toward a region where L_B is low. Nothing in this process cares about L_A. Unless the low-loss regions for A and B happen to overlap and the optimization happens to stay in the overlap, the weights will leave the good region for A. Because each weight participates in many functions (distributed representations), almost any change affects task A.

When the data for both tasks are available together, the solution is simple: train on a mixture of both (interleaved training), and the optimizer finds weights good for both. Catastrophic forgetting arises when data arrive sequentially and old data are no longer available, which is the normal situation for an animal and for many deployed AI systems (a robot in a changing environment, a model updated with new information).

The stability-plasticity dilemma, mentioned in section 11.2, is the core tension: a system that changes easily (plastic) forgets easily, and a system that resists change (stable) learns slowly.

Measuring continual learning

Researchers evaluate continual learning methods with benchmarks in which a model learns a sequence of tasks or data distributions. Common scenarios, as described by Gido van de Ven and Andreas Tolias in 2019 and later work, include:

- Task-incremental learning: the model is told which task it is performing at test time.
- Domain-incremental learning: the task structure stays the same but the input distribution changes (for example, recognizing digits written in different styles).
- Class-incremental learning: new classes are added over time, and the model must distinguish among all classes seen so far without being told which task a test example comes from. This is the hardest scenario.

Typical metrics include average accuracy across all tasks after training on the whole sequence, the amount of forgetting (drop in accuracy on old tasks), and forward and backward transfer (whether learning a task helps future or past tasks).

Family 1: replay

The most effective general strategy is replay: mix old experiences with new ones during training.

- Experience replay (rehearsal): store a small buffer of examples from old tasks and include them in training batches for new tasks. Even a small buffer helps substantially.
- Generative replay: train a generative model to produce samples resembling old data, and replay those samples instead of storing real examples (Hanul Shin and colleagues, 2017). This avoids storing raw data, which can matter for privacy or memory limits.
- Brain-inspired replay: van de Ven, Hava Siegelmann, and Tolias proposed in 2020 replaying internal representations (hidden-layer activity) generated by the network's own feedback connections rather than raw inputs, inspired by the observation that the hippocampus replays abstract, compressed representations.

Brain analog: hippocampal replay during sleep and rest, which interleaves recent experiences with older knowledge and supports consolidation in the neocortex (section 9.2), exactly as complementary learning systems theory proposed.

Family 2: regularization (protecting important weights)

A second strategy is to identify the weights most important for old tasks and make them resistant to change.

- Elastic weight consolidation (EWC), introduced by James Kirkpatrick, Razvan Pascanu, and colleagues at DeepMind in a 2017 PNAS paper, adds a penalty to the loss when learning task B:

  L(w) = L_B(w) + sum over i of (lambda / 2) * F_i * (w_i - w_A,i)^2

  where w_A is the weight vector after learning task A, F_i is the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix (an estimate of how much the loss on task A depends on weight i), and lambda sets the strength of protection. Weights important for A behave as if attached to their old values by stiff springs; unimportant weights are free to change. The "elastic" name comes from this spring analogy, and the authors explicitly motivated the method by studies showing that some dendritic spines are stabilized after learning while others remain plastic.

- Synaptic intelligence (Friedemann Zenke, Ben Poole, and Surya Ganguli, 2017) estimates each weight's importance online, by accumulating how much it contributed to reducing the loss during training, and uses a similar quadratic penalty. The authors framed this as giving each synapse a richer internal state, motivated by the biological complexity of synapses.

- Memory aware synapses and related methods estimate importance from the sensitivity of the network's outputs to each weight.

Brain analog: the stable scaffold of synapses with a plastic minority (section 11.2), synaptic tagging and consolidation (section 7.2), and theoretical work on synapses with multiple internal states. Stefano Fusi, Patrick Drew, and Larry Abbott proposed in 2005 the "cascade model" of synapses, in which each synapse has a chain of hidden states with progressively lower plasticity, so that frequently reinforced synapses become harder to change. Marcus Benna and Fusi extended this in 2016 with a model of synapses as interacting variables with multiple time scales, and showed theoretically that such complex synapses can greatly increase memory capacity and lifetime compared with simple synapses. These theories suggest that the molecular complexity of real synapses may be a solution to the stability-plasticity dilemma.

Family 3: architectural approaches (separating resources)

A third strategy is to use different parts of the network for different tasks.

- Progressive neural networks (Rusu and colleagues, 2016) add a new column of units for each new task, with lateral connections to old columns, which are frozen. Nothing is forgotten, but the network grows with each task.
- Parameter isolation methods, such as PackNet (Arun Mallya and Svetlana Lazebnik, 2018), prune the network after each task and reuse freed weights for the next task, keeping the important weights for old tasks fixed.
- Context-dependent gating: Nicolas Masse, Gregory Grant, and David Freedman proposed in 2018 multiplying hidden units by a task-specific sparse binary mask, so that each task uses a different, partially overlapping subset of units. This was inspired by the idea that context signals in the brain (for example, from prefrontal cortex) might gate which neurons are active.
- Mixture-of-experts architectures, widely used in modern large models for efficiency, route each input to a subset of "expert" subnetworks, which can reduce interference between different kinds of data.

Brain analog: sparse coding and pattern separation in the hippocampus (section 9.1), which assign distinct sets of neurons to distinct memories; adult neurogenesis (section 11.2), which might add fresh units; and the modular organization of the cortex into specialized areas (chapter 3). In the fruit fly, the mushroom body, a learning center, uses a very sparse code in which each odor activates a small fraction of thousands of Kenyon cells, and dopamine neurons modulate plasticity in separate compartments; theoretical studies, such as work by Yang Shen, Sanjoy Dasgupta, and Saket Navlakha (2023), have argued that this architecture helps flies learn new associations without forgetting old ones and have used it to design continual learning algorithms.

Family 4: optimization-based approaches

Some methods modify the gradient updates themselves so they interfere less with old tasks. For example, gradient episodic memory (David Lopez-Paz and Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, 2017) stores examples from old tasks and projects new gradients so that they do not increase the loss on those examples. Orthogonal gradient descent and related methods constrain updates to directions orthogonal to those important for previous tasks. These have a loose brain analog in the idea that new learning might be routed into "null spaces" of neural activity that do not affect existing outputs, an idea discussed in the motor control literature. Matthew Kaufman, Mark Churchland, Stephen Ryu, and Krishna Shenoy proposed in 2014 that motor cortex prepares movements in an "output-null" subspace of activity that does not drive muscles, which illustrates how a network can change internally without disturbing its output.

Continual learning in large models

For large language models and other foundation models, continual learning takes new forms. These models are trained once on massive datasets and then adapted. When they are fine-tuned on new data, they can lose general capabilities, an effect related to catastrophic forgetting. Practitioners mitigate this by mixing in some original pretraining data (replay), by using parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA (low-rank adaptation, introduced by Edward Hu and colleagues in 2021), which add small trainable matrices while freezing the original weights (an architectural approach), and by retrieval augmentation, which supplies new information through external memory rather than changing weights at all (section 9.4). Interestingly, very large pretrained models appear to suffer less from catastrophic forgetting in some settings than small models trained from scratch, possibly because their rich representations allow new tasks to be learned with smaller changes. But how to keep a large model's knowledge current over long periods, without periodic expensive retraining, remains an open problem.

What the brain still does better

Despite progress, no AI system yet matches the brain's ability to learn continually over decades, from a single stream of experience, without forgetting important knowledge, while remaining energy efficient. The brain appears to combine all four families of solutions:

- Replay: sleep and rest replay in the hippocampus and cortex.
- Regularization: synaptic consolidation with complex, multi-state synapses.
- Architecture: sparse codes, modularity, neurogenesis, and context-dependent gating by neuromodulators and prefrontal signals.
- Optimization: learning in subspaces that minimize interference, and plasticity controlled by attention and reward.

In addition, the brain uses complementary learning systems (a fast hippocampus and a slow neocortex), forgets selectively in ways that may aid generalization, and leverages strong innate structure from evolution. A 2022 review in Nature Machine Intelligence by Dhireesha Kudithipudi and a large group of coauthors, "Biological underpinnings for lifelong learning machines," surveyed these mechanisms and argued that combining several of them will be needed for truly lifelong learning machines.

An engineering view

For a mechatronics student, continual learning is not an abstract problem. A robot deployed in a home or factory will face new objects, new tasks, and changing conditions. Retraining it from scratch every time is impractical. Practical systems often use a combination of a frozen, general perception backbone (like stable early sensory cortex), a small set of trainable task-specific components (like plastic higher areas), a buffer of past experiences for replay (like a hippocampus), and careful monitoring of performance on old tasks (like the brain's checks through behavior). Designing such systems is an active area of robotics research, and the brain provides one of the few existence proofs that the problem can be solved well.

Summary

- Neural networks trained sequentially on tasks forget earlier tasks (catastrophic forgetting) because shared weights are moved away from regions good for old tasks.
- Continual learning benchmarks include task-, domain-, and class-incremental scenarios.
- Replay (stored, generated, or internal representations) is highly effective and mirrors hippocampal replay.
- Regularization methods such as EWC and synaptic intelligence protect important weights, inspired by synaptic consolidation and complex multi-state synapses.
- Architectural methods (progressive networks, parameter isolation, context-dependent gating, mixture of experts) separate resources, resembling sparse coding, modularity, neurogenesis, and the fly mushroom body.
- Optimization methods project updates to avoid interference, related to null-space ideas in motor cortex.
- Large models use replay, LoRA, and retrieval augmentation; lifelong learning comparable to the brain remains an open challenge.
